However, the NATA fears that carriers which do hold such certificates will now be able to serve plants which are outside the present commercial zones but within the proposed expanded zones and divert traffic from the carriers presently serving those plants. It is argued that if many carriers are authorized to serve a particular plantsite in initial movements, carriers illequipped to perform the service will solicit business offering lower rates. Traffic will be diverted from existing carriers, depriving them of the revenues they need to maintain their facilities, and service to the public will deteriorate. NATA urges that if the Commission decides to adopt the proposed expansion of commercial zones and terminal areas, that it exempt the terminal areas of initial movement automobile carriers from this expansion.
The National Tank Truck Carriers, Inc., (NTTC) submitted representations on behalf of motor carriers engaged in the transportation of liquid and dry commodities in bulk. It states that the nature of the transportation of commodities in bulk is such that the commodities often are not transported a great distance. It argues that expansion of commercial zones will result in deregulation of a substantial portion of the tank truck industry, particularly in the vicinity of major cities, and that such deregulation will mean that the Commission's safety regulations will no longer apply to these operations.
